title: Chemistry IX · 2017 · E-Marking Notes (Questions & Solved Better Responses)
subject: Chemistry
introduction: This document has been produced for the teachers and candidates of Secondary School Certificate (SSC-I) Chemistry. It contains official comments on candidates' responses to the May 2017 SSC-I Examination indicating the quality of the responses and highlighting their relative strengths and weaknesses.
generalObservations: In comparison to previous years, candidates attempted the paper well. However, there is still room for improvement. Key concepts that teachers need to focus on and give candidates more drill and practice include: (a) Balancing and construction of chemical equations and ionic equations, (b) Drawing of dot and cross structures representing different types of chemical bonds, (c) Drawing of atomic structures for different elements, ions and atoms of isotopes, and (d) Problem solving which involves use of correct formula, manipulation of formula as per the data given and substitution of values to obtain the correct answer.

questions.questionText:
Given below is a chemical equation showing the reaction between magnesium ribbon and oxygen gas.
Mg(s) + O2(g) -> X
a. Identify the product X and balance the given chemical equation. (2 Marks)
b. Name the type of chemical reaction taking place in this equation. (1 Mark)
questions.sloText: Identify types of chemical reactions and write balanced chemical equations.
checkingHints: Part a (2 marks): Product X = MgO (1 mark); Balanced equation: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO (1 mark).
Part b (1 mark): Addition / synthesis / combination / combustion / oxidation reaction.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses accurately identified product X as MgO, balanced the equation as 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO, and named the reaction type (addition, synthesis, combination, combustion, or oxidation). Weaker responses wrote incorrect formulas like Mg3O2 and misidentified the reaction as reduction or displacement.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses showed correct identification of product X with accurate balancing of the given equation. Furthermore, candidates identified the type of chemical reaction using multiple valid names such as combustion reaction, oxidation reaction, addition reaction, synthesis reaction, or combination reaction.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses demonstrated poor conceptual knowledge about the type of chemical reactions. A few displayed correct identification of the product but failed to balance the equation and name the type of chemical reaction, writing incorrect reaction types such as reduction, covalent bond, transitional reaction, or displacement reaction.
suggestions: Ensure students deduce chemical formulas using ionic valencies (Mg2+ and O2- -> MgO) before attempting to balance stoichiometric coefficients.
Review classification of chemical reactions (addition/synthesis, decomposition, single/double displacement, combustion).
questions.modelAnswer:
a. Product X is MgO. Balanced equation: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO.
b. Addition / synthesis / combination / combustion reaction.

questions.questionText:
Complete the table for the given substances (Dot and Cross Diagram):
- Oxygen gas
- Nitrogen gas
- Methane gas
- Carbon dioxide gas
questions.sloText: Draw dot and cross structures for simple covalent molecules.
checkingHints: 1 mark each for accurate dot-and-cross diagrams of O2 (double bond), N2 (triple bond), CH4 (four single bonds), and CO2 (two double bonds).
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses drew clear overlapping or Lewis dot-and-cross diagrams showing the exact number of shared bonding pairs and unshared lone pairs for O2, N2, CH4, and CO2. Weaker responses confused methane (CH4) with ammonia (NH3) or drew incorrect valence electron counts for CO2.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses managed to draw the dot and cross structures of the given substances highlighting the correct number of valence electrons and proper sharing of electrons between atoms (O=O double bond, N≡N triple bond, cuatro single C–H bonds in CH4, and O=C=O double bonds in CO2).
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses failed to draw the correct dot and cross structures for all four substances. A few drew accurate structures for oxygen and nitrogen but confused methane with NH3 or drew wrong valence electron counts for carbon dioxide.
suggestions: Have students first write the molecular formula and count valence electrons (8 - Group number = number of covalent bonds needed) before drawing dot-and-cross structures.
Always check that every main-group atom (C, N, O) has a complete octet of 8 electrons after sharing.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Oxygen gas (O2): Double covalent bond (2 shared pairs) with 2 lone pairs on each O.
- Nitrogen gas (N2): Triple covalent bond (3 shared pairs) with 1 lone pair on each N.
- Methane gas (CH4): Central C sharing 4 single covalent bonds with 4 H atoms.
- Carbon dioxide gas (CO2): Central C forming two double covalent bonds (O=C=O) with 2 lone pairs on each O.

questions.questionText:
Consider the given structure of an atom of an element X (2 p, 2 n, 2 electrons in K shell) to answer the following questions.
a. Identify the element X. (1 Mark)
b. Name another element belonging to the same group as element X. (1 Mark)
c. State any THREE properties that all the elements of this group have in common. (3 Marks)
questions.sloText: Identify elements from atomic structure and state common properties of Group VIIIA noble gases.
checkingHints: Part a (1 mark): Helium (He).
Part b (1 mark): Neon / Argon / Krypton / Xenon / Radon.
Part c (3 marks): Any 3 common properties of noble gases (complete valence shell, unreactive/inert, monoatomic colourless gases).
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses recognized the 2-proton, 2-electron atom as Helium (He), named another noble gas like Argon or Neon, and listed three shared properties of Group VIIIA. Weaker responses misidentified the atom as Beryllium (confusing 2 valence electrons in K-shell with Group IIA) and carried that error into parts b and c.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses accurately identified element X as Helium (He), named another element such as neon, argon, krypton, xenon, or radon from Group VIIIA, and stated three distinctive properties common to noble gases (colourless monoatomic gases, complete outer electron shell, chemically unreactive with zero valency).
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses showed poor understanding about the characteristics of different groups. They misidentified the element in part 'a' as beryllium, calcium, or hydrogen, then mentioned magnesium or sodium in part 'b' and gave Group I or II metallic properties in part 'c'.
suggestions: Highlight the special position of Helium (Z=2): although it has 2 valence electrons, its K-shell is completely full (duplet), placing it in Group VIIIA (noble gases), not Group IIA.
Drill element identification using proton count (Z) in the nucleus.
questions.currentTopic: Periodic Table & Group VIIIA Noble Gases
questions.modelAnswer:
a. Helium (He).
b. Argon (Ar) or Neon (Ne).
c. 1. They do not react with any other element (chemically inert).
2. They have a complete outermost electron shell (duplet/octet).
3. They are all monoatomic colourless gases known as noble gases.

questions.questionText:
i. State the relationship between volume and temperature of a gas presented by J. Charles. (1 Mark)
ii. Give mathematical representation of Charles's law to support your answer in part i. (1 Mark)
questions.sloText: State Charles's law and write its mathematical expression.
checkingHints: Part i (1 mark): Volume of a given mass of gas is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant pressure.
Part ii (1 mark): V ∝ T  or  V/T = k  or  V1/T1 = V2/T2.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses stated the direct proportionality between gas volume and temperature at constant pressure and wrote V ∝ T (V1/T1 = V2/T2). Weaker responses confused Charles's law with Boyle's law, stating an inverse relationship (V ∝ 1/T or VT = k).
questions.betterResponses: Better responses correctly stated the law of J. Charles regarding the direct relationship between volume and temperature at constant pressure, accompanied by the accurate mathematical expression V ∝ T and V1/T1 = V2/T2.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses exhibited confusion between Boyle's law and Charles's law, stating an inverse relationship between volume and temperature (V ∝ 1/T) or relating volume and pressure.
suggestions: Use everyday thermal expansion examples (hot air balloons rising, inflated balloon expanding in warm water) to anchor Charles's direct proportionality V ∝ T.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Volume of a given mass of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature when pressure is kept constant.
ii. V ∝ T  =>  V = kT  =>  V1 / T1 = V2 / T2.

questions.questionText:
A doctor prescribed milk of magnesia, a suspension of magnesium hydroxide, to a patient in order to be used as a neutraliser for stomach acidity.
How would you determine that milk of magnesia is a suspension? Give THREE reasons. (3 Marks)
questions.sloText: Compare the physical characteristics of solutions, colloids, and suspensions.
checkingHints: 1 mark for each of any 3 valid reasons (total 3 marks):
- Particles are large (> 10^-5 cm) and visible to the naked eye.
- Particles do not dissolve completely and form a heterogeneous mixture (settle down on standing).
- Particles cannot pass through filter paper (separated by filtration).
- Mixture is opaque and blocks light.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses listed three concrete physical criteria of suspensions: large particles visible to the naked eye, heterogeneous nature with undissolved particles settling out, and retention on filter paper. Weaker responses confused suspensions with true solutions ('particles are easily dissolved') or wrote irrelevant medical statements.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses interpreted the given information correctly and gave distinctive characteristics proving magnesium hydroxide is a suspension: heterogeneous mixture, opaque appearance, particles larger than 10^-5 cm visible to the naked eye, and particles unable to pass through filter paper.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses presented characteristics of true solutions ('particles are easily dissolved') or wrote irrelevant statements like 'it is made of milk' or 'works as a base that neutralises stomach acidity'.
suggestions: Conduct a 3-beaker classroom comparison of salt water (solution), starch/milk (colloid), and chalk/magnesia in water (suspension), testing filtration, settling, and light transmission.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Its particles are large enough (> 10^-5 cm) to be seen with the naked eye.
2. Its particles do not dissolve completely and form a heterogeneous opaque mixture that settles on standing.
3. Its particles cannot pass through filter paper and leave a residue upon filtration.

questions.questionText: 150 cm3 of an aqueous sodium chloride solution contains 3 g sodium chloride. Calculate the mass/volume percentage of the given solution. (2 Marks)
questions.sloText: Calculate the percentage composition (% m/v) of a solution.
checkingHints: 1 mark for formula and substitution: % m/v = (3 g / 150 cm3) × 100.
1 mark for final answer: 2%.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses stated the % (m/v) formula, substituted 3 g and 150 cm3, and computed 2%. Weaker responses inverted the fraction (150 / 3 × 100 = 5000%) or unnecessarily converted cm3 to dm3.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses showed in-depth understanding of percentage composition of solutions and calculated the correct mass by volume percentage (2%) using % m/v = (mass of solute / volume of solution) × 100.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses used inverted formulas (dividing volume by mass: 150 / 3 × 100 = 5000), forgot to multiply by 100, or performed unnecessary unit conversions to dm3 or kg.
suggestions: Emphasize that percentage concentration formulas (% m/v) explicitly use grams (g) and cubic centimetres (cm3 / mL) without converting to dm3.
questions.modelAnswer:
% m/v = (Mass of solute (g) / Volume of solution (cm3)) × 100
% m/v = (3 g / 150 cm3) × 100 = 2%.

questions.questionText: If 15 cm3 of 5 M hydrochloric acid solution has been diluted to 100 cm3, then what will be the molarity of the prepared solution? (2 Marks)
questions.sloText: Calculate the molarity of diluted solutions using M1V1 = M2V2.
checkingHints: 1 mark for dilution equation M1V1 = M2V2 => 5 × 15 = M2 × 100.
1 mark for final answer: M2 = 0.75 M.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses organized the given data, applied M1V1 = M2V2, and solved M2 = (15 × 5) / 100 = 0.75 M. Weaker responses wrote the formula correctly but subtracted instead of dividing (100 - 75 = 25 M).
questions.betterResponses: Better responses demonstrated clarity about the dilution of solutions from concentrated stock solutions and calculated M2 = 0.75 M using M1V1 = M2V2.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses displayed weak algebraic skills—substituting 15 × 5 = 100 × M2 but then subtracting (100 - 75 = 25 M) instead of dividing 75 by 100.
suggestions: Train students to isolate the unknown variable algebraically (M2 = M1V1 / V2) before plugging in numbers.

questions.questionText:
An element X has relative atomic number of 11. It loses one electron and acquires +1 oxidation state. It gives a violent reaction with cold water.
a. Identify element X based on the given characteristics. (1 Mark)
b. Which period of the periodic table does element X belong to? (1 Mark)
c. What products are formed on reaction of element X with cold water? (2 Marks)
questions.sloText: Identify alkali metals and describe their position in the periodic table and reaction with cold water.
checkingHints: Part a (1 mark): Sodium (Na).
Part b (1 mark): 3rd period.
Part c (2 marks): Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and Hydrogen gas (H2) / 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses identified Z=11 as Sodium, deduced Period 3 from its 3 electron shells (2, 8, 1), and wrote the balanced equation 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2. Weaker responses confused group number (1) with period number (3) and wrote observations ('gives a violent reaction') instead of chemical products.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses identified element X as Sodium, gauged the 3rd period from its electronic configuration, and worked out the products by writing the balanced equation 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses identified sodium in part 'a' but wrote Period 1 in part 'b' (confusing group number with period number) and wrote physical observations ('gives a violent reaction') instead of chemical products in part 'c'.
suggestions: Reinforce the distinction between Period Number (= number of electron shells, 3 for Na) and Group Number (= number of valence electrons, 1 for Na).
Clarify that 'what products are formed' requires chemical names or formulas (sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas), not physical observations.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. Sodium (Na).
b. 3rd period.
c. Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and hydrogen gas (H2): 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2.

questions.questionText:
i. Mention any FOUR medical uses of isotopes of any element. (4 Marks)
ii. Draw the atomic structures of three isotopes of oxygen, specifying their number of protons, neutrons and electrons. (4 Marks)
questions.sloText: Describe medical applications of radioactive isotopes and draw atomic structures of isotopes.
checkingHints: Part i (4 marks): Any 4 valid medical uses of radioisotopes (P-32/Sr-90 for skin cancer, Co-60 for internal cancer radiotherapy, I-131 for thyroid goiter, Tc-99m for bone growth, Na-24 for blood circulation).
Part ii (4 marks): Specifying p=8, e=8, and n=8, 9, 10 for 16_8 O, 17_8 O, and 18_8 O, and drawing their 3 atomic structures.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses detailed four specific medical applications naming the exact radioisotopes (P-32, Sr-90, Co-60, I-131, Tc-99m) and drew clean comparative tables and Bohr diagrams for 16_8 O, 17_8 O, and 18_8 O. Weaker responses wrote general biological uses of ordinary oxygen gas ('patients with asthma use oxygen to breathe') and miscounted protons/electrons in the isotope drawings.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses specified four medical uses of radioisotopes (Co-60 for internal tumours, P-32 and Sr-90 for skin cancer, I-131 for goiter in the thyroid gland, Tc-99m for monitoring bone growth) and drew accurate atomic structures for 16_8 O (p=8, e=8, n=8), 17_8 O (p=8, e=8, n=9), and 18_8 O (p=8, e=8, n=10).
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses confused medical uses of radioactive isotopes with breathing oxygen gas for asthma, or drew isotopes of hydrogen/carbon instead of oxygen, or changed the proton and electron counts across the three oxygen isotopes.
suggestions: Teach medical radioisotopes with a structured table: Isotope Name -> Radiation Emitted -> Medical Diagnostic/Therapeutic Application.
Remind students that all isotopes of an element have the exact same number of protons and electrons; only the neutron count in the nucleus changes.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Medical Uses:
1. P-32 and Sr-90 emit beta radiations used to treat skin cancer.
2. Co-60 emits gamma rays used to destroy internal cancer tumours.
3. I-131 is used for the diagnosis and treatment of goiter in the thyroid gland.
4. Technetium-99m is used to monitor bone growth.
ii. Three Isotopes of Oxygen:
- 16_8 O: p+ = 8, e- = 8, n0 = 8 (K=2, L=6)
- 17_8 O: p+ = 8, e- = 8, n0 = 9 (K=2, L=6)
- 18_8 O: p+ = 8, e- = 8, n0 = 10 (K=2, L=6)

questions.questionText:
Given are the atomic structures of calcium and chlorine. These two elements form a compound called calcium chloride.
i. Name the bond that joins calcium and chlorine atoms together. (1 Mark)
ii. Explain the formation of bond between calcium and chlorine atoms. (6 Marks)
iii. Draw a dot and cross diagram to represent the bond in calcium chloride. (1 Mark)
questions.sloText: Explain the formation of ionic bonds in calcium chloride (CaCl2) and draw its dot-and-cross structure.
checkingHints: Part i (1 mark): Ionic bond.

Part ii (6 marks): Stepwise explanation of Ca (2 valence electrons) transferring 1 electron to each of two Cl atoms (7 valence electrons each) to form Ca^(2+) cation and two Cl^- anions held by electrostatic attraction.
Part iii (1 mark): Dot-and-cross structure of CaCl2 showing charges and octets.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses identified the ionic bond, explained why one calcium atom requires two chlorine atoms to accept its two valence electrons, and drew the dot-and-cross diagram with +2 and -1 ionic charges. Weaker responses misidentified the bond as coordinate covalent (using 'donor' and 'acceptor' terminology) and failed to show two chloride ions.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses identified the ionic bond, gave an in-depth explanation of complete electron transfer from electropositive calcium (losing 2 valence electrons) to two electronegative chlorine atoms (each gaining 1 electron) to form Ca^(2+) cations and Cl^- anions, and drew an accurate dot-and-cross representation.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses misidentified the bonding in CaCl2 as covalent or coordinate covalent, using 'lone pair donor/acceptor' terminology instead of ionic electron transfer, and drew only a single chlorine atom without ionic charges.
suggestions: Clarify that 'donor/acceptor' terminology belongs strictly to coordinate covalent (dative) bonding where a lone pair is shared, whereas metal + non-metal bonding is Ionic Bonding via complete electron transfer.
Show stoichiometry visually: 1 Ca atom (2 valence e-) must pair with 2 Cl atoms (each needing 1 e-) to form CaCl2.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Ionic bond.
ii. Calcium is an electropositive metal with 2 electrons in its outermost shell, while chlorine is an electronegative non-metal with 7 valence electrons needing 1 electron to complete its octet. One calcium atom completely transfers its 2 valence electrons—one to each of two chlorine atoms. Calcium becomes a positively charged cation (Ca^(2+)) and each chlorine atom becomes a negatively charged anion (Cl^-), forming CaCl2.
iii. Dot and cross diagram: [Cl]^- [Ca]^(2+) [Cl]^-.

questions.questionText:
i. Define amorphous and crystalline solids. (2 Marks)
ii. Differentiate between gases and solids on the basis of the following properties. (5 Marks)
• Volume
• Compressibility
• Density
• Boiling point
• Ease of flow
questions.sloText: Define amorphous and crystalline solids and differentiate between gases and solids.
checkingHints: Part i (2 marks): Definitions of amorphous and crystalline solids with examples.
Part ii (5 marks): 1 mark each for contrasting gases and solids across Volume, Compressibility, Density, Boiling point, and Ease of flow.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses defined both solid types with examples and constructed a neat two-column table contrasting gases and solids across all five parameters. Weaker responses contradicted themselves in part 'i' (claiming amorphous solids have sharp melting points) and compared gases with liquids instead of solids in part 'ii'.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses correctly defined amorphous and crystalline solids with examples (plastic, rubber, glass vs. diamond, NaCl) and tabulated clear distinguishing points between gases and solids across volume, compressibility, density, boiling point, and ease of flow.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses contradicted their own definitions of amorphous solids and compared gases with liquids rather than gases with solids in part 'ii', or wrote generic definitions of the five properties without contrasting the two states.
suggestions: Train students to always use a side-by-side comparative table whenever a question uses the command word 'Differentiate between X and Y on the basis of...'.
Verify that students read the exact pair of states requested (Gases vs. Solids, not Gases vs. Liquids).
questions.currentTopic: States of Matter & Properties of Solids and Gases
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Amorphous solids have irregularly arranged particles and no sharp melting points (e.g. plastic, rubber, glass). Crystalline solids have regularly arranged particles in a 3D lattice and sharp melting points (e.g. diamond, NaCl).
ii. Gases vs. Solids:
- Volume: Gases have no fixed volume; Solids have fixed volume.
- Compressibility: Gases are highly compressible; Solids are incompressible.
- Density: Gases have lowest density (g/dm3); Solids have high density (g/cm3).
- Boiling point: Gases have low boiling points; Solids have high boiling points.
- Ease of flow: Gases flow easily; Solids cannot flow (only vibrate).

questions.questionText:
The given diagram shows an electrolytic cell that is used for refining of copper.
i. Name the anode, cathode and electrolyte used for the given electrolytic cell. (3 Marks)
ii. How is copper purified through the process of electrolytic refining? Support your answer using balanced chemical equation for the reactions occurring at the anode and the cathode. (4 Marks)
questions.sloText: Describe the electrolytic refining of copper with balanced electrode equations.
checkingHints: Part i (3 marks): Anode = Impure/blistered copper (1 mark); Cathode = Pure copper (1 mark); Electrolyte = Aqueous CuSO4 solution (1 mark).

Part ii (4 marks): Process description including anode dissolution, Cu^(2+) migration/deposition on cathode, and anode mud (2 marks); Anode equation Cu -> Cu^(2+) + 2e^- (1 mark); Cathode equation Cu^(2+) + 2e^- -> Cu (1 mark).
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses labeled the anode as impure/blistered copper, the cathode as pure copper, and the electrolyte as CuSO4, explained the dissolution of Cu^(2+) from the anode, settling of Ag/Au anode mud, and deposition of 99.99% pure copper at the cathode, and wrote balanced half-equations. Weaker responses confused electrolytic refining of copper with electroplating copper onto an iron object.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses demonstrated correct identification of anode (impure/blistered copper), cathode (pure copper), and electrolyte (CuSO4). Candidates explained the stepwise loss of electrons at the anode, settling of anode mud containing Ag and Au, and gain of electrons to deposit 99.99% pure copper at the cathode, supported by balanced half-equations.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses confused the electrolytic refining of copper with electroplating of copper onto iron, identifying the cathode as an iron plate and writing erroneous equations involving Fe^(2+) ions.
suggestions: Clearly contrast Electrolytic Refining of Copper (Anode = Impure Cu, Cathode = Pure Cu) with Electroplating of Copper (Anode = Pure Cu, Cathode = Object/Iron to be plated).
Emphasize what happens to impurities (anode mud/sludge) during copper refining.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Anode: Impure / blistered copper; Cathode: Pure copper; Electrolyte: Copper(II) sulphate (CuSO4) solution.
ii. When current flows, copper atoms from the impure anode oxidise into Cu^(2+) ions and dissolve into the CuSO4 electrolyte, while impurities like Ag and Au settle as anode mud. The cathode attracts Cu^(2+) ions, which get reduced and deposited as 99.99% pure copper:
- At the Anode (Oxidation): Cu -> Cu^(2+) + 2e^-
- At the Cathode (Reduction): Cu^(2+) + 2e^- -> Cu
